questions.explanation: The line inside the box is the median, the middle of the ordered data, and a standard box plot has no mark for the mean anywhere. So 18 tells you the median and nothing about the average. The tempting wrong answer is that the middle line gives the mean, which is a common belief because the line sits in the centre of the picture, but position in a picture is not the same as the average of the values.
questions.hint: Which measure does the line inside the box actually report?
questions.learningObjective: reject the claim that a box plot reports the mean

options.text: The middle line marks the median, and a box plot never shows the mean at all

options.misconception: believes the central line reports the average rather than the middle value
options.text: The middle line marks the mean, because it sits between the two box edges

options.misconception: assumes the average and the middle value are always the same number
options.text: The mean and median always agree, so 18 is confirmed to be the mean

options.misconception: mislabels the middle line as the lower box edge
options.text: The middle line marks the first quartile, so the mean must be 12

questions.explanation: Team A has a mean of 75 against Team B's 70, so A scored higher on average, and Team A's standard deviation is about 3.42 against Team B's 17.08, so A's scores are far less spread out. Both halves of the claim hold, so it is supported. The tempting wrong answer picks the single largest score, 95, to judge consistency, but consistency is about how tightly the scores cluster, not about the top score.
questions.hint: Check the mean for each team, then check the spread for each.
questions.learningObjective: judge a claim that rests on both a mean and a spread comparison

options.misconception: believes the two halves of the claim cannot be checked together
options.text: No, because a higher mean rules out any claim about consistency
